flashcards.q: What is GCP's resource hierarchy order, and how does allow-policy inheritance work?
flashcards.a: Organization -> Folder -> Project -> Resource. Allow policies are additive/union -- the effective policy on a resource is the union of its own bindings plus everything inherited from every ancestor. A child cannot remove or narrow a grant an ancestor made.

flashcards.q: How does GCP's IAM evaluation model differ fundamentally from AWS's?
flashcards.a: AWS evaluates identity policies plus resource policies with explicit Deny winning over any Allow. GCP has no explicit-deny-in-the-allow-policy concept -- it binds roles additively on a resource hierarchy, and the only override is a separate deny policy resource or Organization Policy (a different axis entirely).

flashcards.q: What is a GCP deny policy and what are its limits?
flashcards.a: A separate IAM v2 resource listing principals/permissions to block, evaluated at every hierarchy level, always wins over any allow grant. Limits: 500 deny policies/resource, 500 deny rules/resource, 2,500 total principal appearances/resource.

flashcards.q: What are the hard limits on GCP custom roles?
flashcards.a: 300 custom roles per organization and 300 per project (independent caps -- project-level roles don't count against org cap), up to 3,000 permissions per role, 64KB combined size of title+description+permission names.

flashcards.q: How does Organization Policy differ from IAM?
flashcards.a: IAM controls who can act (grants roles to principals). Organization Policy restricts what configuration is allowed to exist for everyone, regardless of identity (boolean or list constraints). Both must permit an action for it to succeed -- an Owner can still be blocked by an org policy constraint.

flashcards.q: Describe the Workload Identity Federation flow and its critical misconfiguration.
flashcards.a: External OIDC/SAML token -> workload identity pool -> provider (attribute mapping + CEL attribute_condition) -> short-lived STS token -> usually impersonates a real service account. The classic misconfig is a missing or too-broad attribute_condition: without it, any subject the IdP will vouch for (e.g. any repo in a GitHub org) is accepted.

flashcards.q: What are the limits on service account keys and access token lifetime?
flashcards.a: Max 10 keys per service account. Default access token lifetime is 3,600 seconds (1 hour), extendable to 43,200 seconds (12 hours) only via the iam.allowServiceAccountCredentialLifetimeExtension org policy list constraint naming specific service accounts.

flashcards.q: State the key numeric limits on a GCP allow policy.
flashcards.a: 1,500 total principal appearances per policy, 250 unique domains/groups, 12 logic operators per IAM Condition expression, up to 20 role bindings for the same role+principal pair with different condition expressions.

flashcards.q: Why can granting Viewer on a resource be a complete no-op?
flashcards.a: Basic roles are concentric: Owner contains Editor's permissions, Editor contains Viewer's. If a principal already has Editor inherited from a parent, granting Viewer at a child resource adds nothing -- the inherited Editor already includes every Viewer permission.

flashcards.q: What is a Principal Access Boundary (PAB) policy and how does it differ from a deny policy?
flashcards.a: A PAB policy is a hard ceiling on the maximum resources a principal can ever access, regardless of what any allow policy grants (conceptually close to an AWS permission boundary). A deny policy blocks specific permissions; a PAB policy caps overall scope. Limits: 500 rules/policy, 10 policies/resource, 1,000/org.

flashcards.q: What problem does Privileged Access Manager (PAM) solve on GCP?
flashcards.a: Just-in-time, time-boxed, approval-gated elevated access, replacing standing Owner/write grants for compliance-sensitive resources like production payment data. It provides an entitlement catalog, approval workflow, automatic expiry, and audit trail that static IAM Conditions with time bounds don't provide on their own.

flashcards.q: Does GCP support resource-based policies like AWS S3 bucket policies?
flashcards.a: Partially -- many services (Cloud Storage buckets, Pub/Sub topics, BigQuery datasets) support resource-level allow-policy bindings, but architecturally these are just another node in the same additive resource hierarchy, not a structurally separate policy type intersected against an identity policy the way AWS evaluates bucket policies.
